Commencement
May 13, 14, and 15, 1994
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into either the Arena or Shryock Auditorium
either by degree candidates or guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal
with alcohol or other distracting objects.
Commencement
May 13, 14, and 15, 1994
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of
society. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the
nation.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help
students learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor
activities for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to
help themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and
counseling; learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political,
and volunteer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-
on projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

IV
Distinguished Service Award
Ivan A. Elliott, Jr.
Ivan A. Elliott, Jr., a distinguished attorney in the State of Illinois for more than four
decades, served as a member of the Southern Illinois University Board of Trustees
from 1967 to 1991. During that time, he was chairman of the Board from 1973 to 1977,
vice chairman of the Board from 1971 to 1972 and 1977 to 1978, and chairman of the
finance committee from 1980 to 1991.
During his years of service on the Board of Trustees, Mr. Elliott represented the
University on the Merit Board and the State Universities Civil Service System from
1968 to 1991 and served as chairman of the Merit Board twice — from 1969 to 1978 and
from 1981 to 1991. He also served on the Illinois Board of Higher Education from 1973
to 1977, the board of directors of the Southern Illinois University Foundation from 1968
to 1991, and the executive committee of the foundation board from 1970 to 1991.
Mr. Elliott was born on October 31, 1923, in Carmi, Illinois. A product of the Carmi
public schools, he took his Bachelor of Arts degree in political science with highest
honors in 1948 and his Doctor of Law degree with honors in 1950 from the University of
Illinois at Urbana. His scholastic honors include membership in Phi Beta Kappa, Phi
Kappa Phi, and the Golden Key National Honor Society.
A practicing attorney with Conger and Elliott, Carmi, since 1952, Mr. Elliott has
been admitted to practice before the Supreme Court of Illinois, the Supreme Court of
the United States, the Court of Appeals of the 7th Circuit and the District Court of the
Southern District of Illinois. He has been listed in The Best Lawyers in America from
1983 to the present.
Mr. Elliott is a member of numerous professional, civic, and church organizations
and has published more than twenty professional articles. His business interests have
included service as director of the First National Bank, Carmi, since 1974, director and
president of the White County Abstract Company since 1966, and director of the Carmi
Times Publishing Company from 1966 to 1974.
In nominating him for this award, Harry J. Haynsworth, professor and dean of the
Southern Illinois University School of Law, described Mr. Elliott as "a distinguished
lawyer who has served this University in a number of capacities, including chairman
of the Board, for a long period of time".
In recognition of his contributions to the University, the Board of Trustees, and the
State of Illinois, Southern Illinois University at Carbondale finds it fitting and proper
to present the Distinguished Service Award to Ivan A. Elliott, Jr.
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Science
Ray W. Fuller
Dr. Ray W. Fuller, a Lilly research fellow and adjunct professor of neurobiology at
the Indiana University School of Medicine, is recognized by his peers as "one of the top
neuroscientists in the world," according to Dr. Ronald A. Browning, professor in the
Department of Physiology at Southern Illinois University at Carbondale, who nomi-
nated him for an honorary degree. "Although Dr. Fuller has made numerous contribu-
tions and discoveries that have enhanced our knowledge of brain chemistry, perhaps
his crowning achievement," said Dr. Browning, "is his work that led to the discovery
of Prozac (fluoxetine), which is currently the most widely used drug for the treatment
of mental depression." Along with two other Eli Lilly and Company researchers, Dr.
Fuller received the 1993 Discoverers Award for research leading to the discovery of
Prozac, which was featured on the cover of Newsweek in 1990 as a "breakthrough drug
for depression."
A native of Southern Illinois, Dr. Fuller was born on December 16, 1935, in Don-
gola. He holds two degrees from Southern Illinois University at Carbondale — the
Bachelor of Arts degree in chemistry in 1957 and the Master of Arts degree in microbi-
ology in 1958. He received the Doctor of Philosophy degree in biochemistry from Pur-
due University in 1961 and an honorary Doctor of Science degree from Purdue in 1990.
He is a member of Sigma Xi and Phi Lambda Upsilon honor societies and received the
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale Alumni Achievement Award in 1986.
Dr. Fuller is affiliated with a number of professional societies, including the Amer-
ican Society of Biological Chemists, the American Society for Neurochemistry, the
American Chemistry Society, the American Society for Pharmacology and Experi-
mental Therapeutics, the Society for Neuroscience (past president of the Indianapolis
chapter), and the International Society for Neurochemistry. His scientific service has
included serving on the editorial boards of a dozen scientific journals, refereeing scien-
tific papers for fifty-eight journals, reviewing grant applications for national agencies
including the National Institutes of Health, and chairing international neurochemistry
symposia. Dr. Fuller is also the author of more than four hundred full-length scientific
publications and has published a similar number of abstracts from presentations at sci-
entific meetings.
Concluding his nomination of Dr. Fuller for an honorary degree, Dr. Browning had
this to say: "In summary, Ray W. Fuller exemplifies all that we would want our un-
dergraduate and graduate students to strive for. Few individuals in the world can
achieve what he has accomplished, but he is an excellent role model for those who
strive to be the best they can."
In recognition of his numerous and significant contributions to the fields of physiol-
ogy, neurochemistry, and pharmacology, and particularly of his role in discovering
Prozac, the most widely used drug in the treatment of mental depression, Southern
Illinois University at Carbondale finds it fitting and proper to award the honorary
degree, Doctor of Science, to Ray W. Fuller.
2
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Humane Discourse
Brian P. Lamb
Brian P. Lamb, chairman and chief executive officer of Cable Satellite Public Affairs
Network (C-SPAN), founded the television network in 1979 and has shepherded its
growth to the point where its two channels now serve more than sixty million cable
households twenty-four hours a day "with a daily, unedited chronicle of the nation's
public life," according to a recent New York Times Magazine story by Thomas J.
Meyer. "C-SPAN's technique — self-styled "video verite" — is simply to turn on the
cameras and let them run, providing viewers with uncut proceedings of the U.S.
Congress and its committees, marathon gavel-to-gavel broadcasts of political conven-
tions, wide-ranging coverage of presidential campaigns and political think-tank panel
discussions, showing life as it happens, without commentary, spin or editing," Meyer
wrote. The broadcasts are uninterrupted by commercials. They are paid for by local
cable companies, which offer the service as part of a package of news and entertain-
ment programs.
In nominating Mr. Lamb for an honorary degree, Dr. Joe S. Foote, professor in the
Department of Radio-Television and dean of the College of Mass Communication and
Media Arts at Southern Illinois University at Carbondale, recalled: "In the beginning,
C-SPAN was truly a one-man show. I remember meeting Brian in late 1979, when he
ran C-SPAN from a spartan store-front office in an apartment complex in Arlington,
Virginia." Foote pointed out how Lamb started with coverage of the United States
House of Representatives and then branched out, going international, to cover the
Canadian and British parliaments, the European Parliament, and the Japanese Diet.
He is currently working to integrate C-SPAN into law, journalism, speech, and politi-
cal science classes in American schools and colleges.
Mr. Lamb was born on October 9, 1941, in Lafayette, Indiana. He graduated from
Purdue University in 1963 with a bachelor's degree in speech. After a stint in the
Navy, he returned to Lafayette to work in television, then moved to Washington, D.C.,
where he worked as a freelance reporter for United Press International Audio, as a
Senate press secretary, and as a White House telecommunications policy staffer. In
1974 he started publishing a biweekly newsletter, The Media Report, and then became
Washington bureau chief for CableVision magazine. In 1977 he began seeking support
from cable industry executives for what would eventually become C-SPAN. Starting
with four staffers, it has grown to its present company of 170.
"Brian Lamb has not only developed C-SPAN into the crown jewel of the cable in-
dustry," Dr. Foote concluded, "but he has done so in a way that enhances the principles
of representative democracy he holds dear. He would be an ideal candidate for an
honorary degree from SIUC."
In recognition of his contributions to the field of telecommunications, particularly in
substantially broadening the public's access to wide-ranging, unedited television cov-
erage of national and international political activity, Southern Illinois University at
Carbondale finds it fitting and proper to present the honorary degree, Doctor of
Humane Discourse, to Brian P. Lamb.

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods — the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft tarns
are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no hood is
worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study. Doctor's
caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is worn on
the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and are cus-
tomarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men only.
Southern Illinois University School of Medicine graduates wear gowns of ma-
roon, the color of the university, with black velvet borders and bars, and soft,
eight-point black velvet tarns with green tassels. The lining of the hood is maroon
with a white chevron and the velvet border is green, the color of the discipline of
medicine.

Southern Illinois University
at Carbondale
Commencement
August 6, 1994
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into either the Arena or Shryock Auditorium
either by degree candidates or guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal
with alcohol or other distracting objects.
Commencement
August 6, 1994
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of
society. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the
nation.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help
students learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor
activities for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to
help themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and
counseling; learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political,
and volunteer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-
on projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods— the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft tarns
are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no hood is
worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study. Doctor's
caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is worn on
the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and are cus-
tomarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men only.
Southern Illinois University School of Medicine graduates wear gowns of ma-
roon, the color of the university, with black velvet borders and bars, and soft,
eight-point black velvet tarns with green tassels. The lining of the hood is maroon
with a white chevron and the velvet border is green, the color of the discipline of
medicine.

Commencement
May 12, 13, and 14, 1995
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into either the Arena or Shryock Auditorium
either by degree candidates or guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal
with alcohol or other distracting objects.
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of
society. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the
nation.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help
students learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor
activities for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to
help themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and
counseling; learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political,
and volunteer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-
on projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

Honorary Degree
Doctor of Humane Letters
Professor Charles Richard Johnson
Professor Charles Richard Johnson of the University of Washington at Seattle is
an American novelist, short-story writer, essayist, and cartoonist. A writer
whose balance of philosophy and folklore has been praised since the publication of
his first novel in 1974, Johnson gained prominence when his novel Middle Pas-
sage won the National Book Award in 1990. He noted, in accepting the award,
that he was the first black male to win the prize since Ralph Ellison was cited for
The Invisible Man in 1953.
Born in 1948 in Evanston, Illinois, Johnson began his career as a cartoonist,
and had his work published when he was just 17. His two collections of cartoons,
many of which were published first in the Daily Egyptian at Southern Illinois
University at Carbondale, were acclaimed for their subtle, but pointed, satire of
race relations. Their success led to Charlie's Pad, a 1971 public television series
that Johnson created, co-produced, and hosted.
As an undergraduate at SIUC, Johnson studied under prize- winning novelist
and literary theorist John Gardner (Sunlight Dialogues, Nickel Mountain, Octo-
ber Light), Gardner's concept of "moral fiction," demanding from the author a
near-fanatical commitment to technique, imagination, and ethics, deeply im-
pressed him. Johnson earned a bachelor's degree (1971) and a master's degree
(1973) at SIUC. He published his first novel, Faith and the Good Thing, in 1974,
while starting work on his Ph.D. in phenomenology at the State University of
New York at Stonybrook.
His other principal works are: Black Humor (cartoons, 1970); Half -Past Na-
tion-Time (cartoons, 1972); Oxherding Tale (novel, 1982); The Sorcerer's Appren-
tice (short stories, nominated for the PEN/Faulkner Award, 1986); Being and
Race: Black Writing Since 1970 (essays, 1988); and Middle Passage (1990).
Johnson's works-in-progress include Dreamer, a. novel about Martin Luther
King Jr., the civil rights movement, and the philosophy of non-violence, soon to
be published by Scribners; and The Black Male in America, a forthcoming book
of essays on the current plight of young African- American males that he will co-
edit with John McCluskey Jr. for Indiana University Press.
Like Middle Passage, which chronicles the misadventures in 1830 of 22-year-
old Rutherford Calhoun, a well-educated, mischievous, freed slave from Southern
Illinois, Dreamer also embodies Johnson's love for Southern Illinois, this time
specifically the area around Makanda.
Johnson is former director of the creative writing program at the University
of Washington. In 1990 he was appointed Pollock Professor of English, the first
endowed professorship in creative writing at the University of Washington. He is
a Guggenheim Fellow and a National Endowment for the Arts Fellow. He is edi-
tor of The Seattle Review and is one of three nominating judges for the Pulitzer
Prize in Literature. He has received the Writers Guild Award for his PBS drama,
Booker. He holds an honorary doctorate from Northwestern University. From
SIUC, he has received the Friends of Morris Library Delta Award (1970), Jour-
nalism Alumnus of the Year Award (1981), and the College of Liberal Arts
Alumni Achievement Award (1991).
Johnson has contributed to the establishment of the Charles Johnson Award
for Fiction and Poetry. The award was initiated by SIUC's Ricardo Cruz, assis-
tant professor in English, who nominated Johnson for this honorary degree. Cruz
wrote in his nominating letter: "As his accomplishments, passion, and commit-
ment prove, Johnson is the kind of alumnus that our University can be proud to
honor in the highest degree possible." In seconding the nomination, Richard F.
Peterson, chairperson of the SIUC Department of English, wrote: "Granting
Charles Johnson an honorary degree, inviting him to spring Commencement, and
granting the first Charles Johnson Awards for Fiction and Poetry would be a
wonderful moment for our University, one in which we honor one of our most dis-
tinguished alumni and reward the bright promise of talented student/writers."
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Commercial Science
Sandra Goeken Martis
Sandra Goeken Martis of Oak Brook, Illinois, president of In-Flight Phone Cor-
poration and board chairman and CEO of In-Flight Phone International of Oak-
brook Terrace, is a Chicago-area business executive who has taken an increasing
role in supporting Southern Illinois University at Carbondale during the past
years.
Goeken Martis* connection with the telecommunications industry dates back
to the 1970s, when Goeken Communications began to develop Airfone, the na-
tion's first air-to-ground telephone system. Since then she has become involved in
every phase of building and running a global business, including coordinating and
petitioning for worldwide frequency allocations.
In-Flight Phone is the only air-to-ground telephone company to provide each
airline passenger with a seatback viewing screen and a telephone headset with
full keyboard capabilities. FlightLink permits passengers to transmit and receive
faxes; send data; play games; view city directories, airport maps, and airline
schedules; shop; obtain reservations; and more. More than one thousand aircraft
are so equipped. In-Flight Phone International has affiliations in Canada, Mexico,
Europe, the Middle East, the Far East, and Australia.
In 1984, Goeken Martis was honored as one of the Outstanding Young Women
in America. In 1992, President George Bush nominated her for membership in
the Federal Communications Commission's Small Business Advisory Committee.
Later, she was elected chair of the New Technology Subcommittee. She has ad-
dressed major national and international aeronautical telecommunications forums
in Washington, D.C.; New Orleans, Louisiana; Palm Springs, California; San
Juan, Puerto Rico; and London, England.
Her interest in SIUC began in 1984, when she accompanied her father, John
D. Goeken, then president of Airfone, Inc., to the campus to see him receive the
SIUC Entrepreneur of the Year Award from the College of Business and Admin-
istration (COBA). That same year she became a member of the COBA Advisory
Board. In 1992, she served as president of the advisory board.
Now an adjunct professor in the College of Business and Administration,
Goeken Martis was named SIUC's Chicago Business Leader of the Year in 1993.
She has served on the SIUC Chicagoland Advisory Council's student services
committee, and on September 18, 1994, she was named chair of the Advisory
Council. She presides over 22 volunteers from the Chicago area in enhancing
Chicagoland fund-raising, public relations, and promotion of special events, such
as the recent SIUC 125th Anniversary Gala, at which she served as master of
8
ceremonies and also provided one of the prizes — a five-day, four-night vacation at
her family's villa in Acapulco, Mexico — at a silent auction.
She has hosted two Lake Michigan reception/cruises for the SIU Foundation's
President's Council on the Goeken family yacht and plans to host an advisory
council meeting on the yacht as well. During her tenure as advisory council chair,
she also plans to hold a reception for prospective SIUC students at the family
farm in Oswego, Illinois, and a job fair for SIUC seniors in the Oak Brook area,
where they can meet with Chicagoland employers.
In the past few years, Goeken Martis has made her offices available to
Du Page County Alumni Chapter volunteers for a telefund campaign; has joined
the President's Council; has contacted SIUC alumni in Thailand during a recent
trip there; and has made financial contributions to COB A.
Starting to work in her father's business, Goeken Communications, right after
high school, she holds an honorary bachelor's degree from the College of St.
Francis in Joliet, Illinois, of which she is now a board member. She also serves on
the board of Joliet Junior College. She is married to Paul Goeken Martis (1992),
who is vice president for corporate planning for In-Flight Phone Corporation.
Paul L. Conti, vice president of Alexander & Alexander Inc. of Chicago, pres-
ident of the SIU Foundation Board of Directors, and past president of the SIU
Alumni Association Board of Directors, in nominating Sandra Goeken Martis for
an honorary degree, cited: "her significant leadership in her chosen profession, as
one of corporate America's outstanding women chief executive officers, and her
continuing commitment to and support for Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale."

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods — the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft tarns
are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no hood is
worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study. Doctor's
caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is worn on
the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and are cus-
tomarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men only.
Southern Illinois University School of Medicine graduates wear gowns of ma-
roon, the color of the university, with black velvet borders and bars, and soft,
eight-point black velvet tarns with green tassels. The lining of the hood is maroon
with a white chevron and the velvet border is green, the color of the discipline of
medicine.

Commencement
August 5, 1995
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and Mends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into the Arena either by degree candidates or by
guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal with alcohol or other distract-
ing objects.
Commencement
August 5, 1995
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of
society. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the
nation.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help
students learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor
activities for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to
help themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and
counseling; learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political,
and volunteer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-
on projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

IV
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Commercial Science
George M. C. Fisher
George M. C. Fisher, chairman, president, and chief executive officer of
Eastman Kodak Company, has his roots in Southern Illinois. He was born and
spent his early years in Union County, Illinois. He received a bachelor's de-
gree in engineering from the University of Illinois at Urbana in 1962, and a
master's degree in engineering (1964) and a Ph.D. degree in mathematics
(1966) from Brown University.
From 1965 to 1971 Dr. Fisher worked at Bell Laboratories. In 1971 he
joined Motorola Corporation as director of manufacturing systems, moving
up in 1986 to chairman and chief executive officer. He is credited with the
phenomenal success this Illinois-based telecommunications company experi-
enced in the late 1980s and early 1990s, resulting in an over 400 percent in-
crease in the value of Motorola stock. In late 1993 Dr. Fisher left Motorola to
accept his current position with Eastman Kodak.
Since arriving at Kodak, he has radically restructured the company, re-
turning the focus of its efforts to photographic and imaging systems and di-
vesting it of chemical and health-care divisions. In recent years, the firm's
leadership in the imaging field has been seriously challenged by such
Japanese and European corporations as Fuji and Agfa, and his purpose is to
bring Kodak back to preeminence in the field where it began over a hundred
years ago.
Dr. Fisher brings his experience in the high technology field of telecom-
munications to bear on Kodak's traditional strengths in photographic imag-
ing. He sees the integration of photographic and electronic imaging systems
as an vital part of the new information superhighway. He is committed to
maintaining and enhancing Kodak's leadership in the development of silver-
based photographic materials as well as in the new digital future of photo-
graphic imaging.
In recruiting new management personnel to Kodak, Dr. Fisher makes use
of close personal ties to CEOs of telecommunications companies like Intel,
Microsoft, Apple, IBM, and Motorola. Kodak is engaging in joint ventures
with some of these companies that will insure its future participation in
imaging and communications networks. As this new industry builds, oppor-
tunities for Southern Illinois University at Carbondale graduates will
abound.
The SIUC College of Mass Communication and Media Arts is also a tangi-
ble symbol of excellence in the areas of telecommunications and imaging arts.
The School of Journalism and the departments of Radio-Television and Cin-
ema and Photography have long been recognized as national leaders in their
fields, and the Broadcasting Service has developed a national reputation for
excellence in many facets of public broadcasting. The Department of Cinema
and Photography has received numerous film grants, workshops, and awards
from Kodak, as well as a $25,000 Kodak Endowment Scholarship Award to
support photography students.
In presenting the name of Dr. George M. C. Fisher, Gary Kolb, chairper-
son of the SIUC Department of Cinema and Photography, said: "Dr. Fisher
has proved his ability as a leader in a highly competitive and rapidly chang-
ing industry. He is a visionary CEO who is leading Kodak back to a preemi-
nent position in the imaging marketplace. He has close ties to our region and
to the departments in the College of Mass Communication and Media Arts.
He is a most deserving nominee for an honorary degree."
In recognition of his contributions to the communications industry, particu-
larly in the fast-moving field of photographic imaging, and of his service to
the region of his youth, Southern Illinois University at Carbondale finds it
fitting and proper to present the honorary degree Doctor of Commercial
Science to George M. C. Fischer.

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods — the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft
tarns are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no
hood is worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study.
Doctor's caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is
worn on the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and
are customarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men
only.
Southern Illinois University School of Medicine graduates wear gowns of ma-
roon, the color of the university, with black velvet borders and bars, and soft,
eight-point black velvet tarns with green tassels. The lining of the hood is maroon
with a white chevron and the velvet border is green, the color of the discipline of
medicine.

Commencement
May 10, 11, 12, 1996
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into either the Arena or Shryock Auditorium
either by degree candidates or guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal
with alcohol or other distracting objects.
Commencement
May 10, 11, 12, 1996
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of so-
ciety. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the na-
tion.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help stu-
dents learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor activi-
ties for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to help
themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and counseling;
learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political, and volun-
teer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-on
projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

IV
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Humane Letters
James R. Fornear
James R. Fornear of Marion, Kentucky, Chairman of the Board and Chief Exec-
utive Officer of Res-Care, Inc., is a distinguished alumnus of Southern Illinois
University at Carbondale (Bachelor of Science, 1960 and Master of Science, 1960).
He has been a dedicated supporter of the University for over three decades and
now serves on the board of directors of the SIU Foundation.
Fornear is the founder of Res-Care, which employs 5,500 people at 130 facili-
ties in eleven states and Puerto Rico and provides services to the developmen-
tally disabled, operates Job Corps centers, and offers home-care assistance. The
name Res-Care is derived from the concepts of respect and care, the bases of
Fornear's enterprise. Res-Care now has three divisions: one for persons with dis-
abilities, offering residential support; one for the training of young people, which
has a record of 80 percent job placement; and one for the homebound, which pro-
vides nursing and nutrition services and physical, speech, and vocational therapy.
James Fornear grew up in the small Southern Illinois community of Sesser. As
a student at SIUC, he majored in education and rehabilitation and recreational
therapy. One of his professors, Guy Renzaglia, now retired, who was then direc-
tor of the SIUC Rehabilitation Institute, remains a close friend. In the 1980's
Fornear helped establish a Guy Renzaglia Scholarship Fund for graduate stu-
dents in rehabilitation, which he has since funded as a fully endowed scholarship.
Through Renzaglia, Fornear met William Freeberg (Bachelor of Science, 1942),
then chairman of the SIUC Department of Recreation, who had established a
recreation camp for the developmentally disabled at Little Grassy Lake (now
Touch of Nature). Freeberg persuaded Fornear to work at the camp during his
school years. Fornear now supports an endowed scholarship in Freeberg's name
and provides financial support for Touch of Nature.
Influenced by outstanding role models during his school years, Fornear has
himself become a role model. Among those whose lives he has influenced is Sey-
mour Bryson (Bachelor of Arts, 1959, Master of Science, 1961, and Doctor of Phi-
losophy, 1972). They met thirty-five years ago when Bryson was an assistant di-
rector at Touch of Nature. Now executive assistant for affirmative action to
SIUC Chancellor John C. Guyon, and a member of the board of directors of Res-
Care, Bryson had this to say about Fornear: "He has not let success change him
— he continues to treat all people with respect and dignity".
Fornear worked as a high school guidance counselor after graduating from
SIUC, but missed his work with the handicapped and underprivileged. When
SIUC was awarded a contract to operate the Job Corps Center at Camp Breckin-
ridge, Kentucky, he went to work there as activities and development director.
Dr. Bryson worked for Fornear there for several years. Fornear stayed on at
Camp Breckinridge after the University's affiliation with the project had ended
and decided he could manage such an organization on his own. With borrowed
money, he established Res-Care in 1974 and was awarded a contract to manage
the Whitney Young Job Corps Center at Simpson ville, Kentucky.
A founding member of the President's Council of the SIU Foundation, Fornear
Fornear is also a member of the National Education Association, the American
Association on Mental Deficiency, the American Camping Association, and the
American Management Association. In 1988 he received the Outstanding
Achievement Award from what was then SIUC's College of Human Resources,
and in 1991 he was named SIUC Entrepreneur of the Year. He has agreed to
fund a Medallion Scholarship in the Cornerstone Endowed Scholarship Program,
recently established to attract academically able undergraduates to SIUC.
SIUC Vice Chancellor for Institutional Advancement J. Robert Quatroche, in
nominating Fornear for an honorary degree, cited him "For significant leadership
and success in his chosen profession; as an outstanding corporate leader who em-
braces human care and concern in his business ventures; and for his continuing
commitment and service to, and support for, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale".
In recognition of his contributions to the field of education and rehabilitation
and of his service to the region of his youth, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale finds it fitting and proper to present the honorary degree Doctor of Hu-
mane Letters to James R. Fornear.
2
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Fine Arts
Darwin Reid Payne
Darwin Reid Payne (Bachelor of Science, 1953, Master of Fine Arts, 1955) is a
leading authority in the field of computer graphics, which is currently revolution-
izing the training of scenic designers and the techniques and procedures that de-
signers may use via computer to conceive, present, and document their designs,
working drawings, and other preparatory materials.
His most recent work, Computer Scenographics, published in 1994 by the
Southern Illinois University Press, will be followed by a work on computer-aided
scene painting techniques. Letters from SIUC professor emeritus Marvin
Kleinau; scenic designer Ronald Naversen of the SIUC Department of Theater;
and the Virtus Corporation attest to Payne's expertise in computer-graphic de-
sign. Moreover, six of Payne's published works had already established him as a
leading scholar and textbook author in his field of scenic design, and another
book, which he coedited, reflects his ability as a playwright and illustrator. His
books, all published by the SIU Press, have collectively brought national and in-
ternational recognition to their author, the University, and the Press.
Payne's reputation extends to his artistic ability as a scenic designer. As a
professional designer, his work has been commissioned by a number of universi-
ties and theaters. As a scenic designer and teacher of scenic design for the SIUC
Department of Theater between 1957 and 1983, he created for SIUC audiences at
least a hundred imaginative, practical, technically perfect, and aesthetically
handsome settings for the stage. Since his retirement from SIUC as a full profes-
sor, Payne has worked as a free-lance designer and director for professional the-
aters and theater schools. He is currently an adjunct faculty member at Wake
Forest University and at the North Carolina School of the Arts.
Beyond his publications and professional reputation, Payne made a substantial
contribution to the University as an outstanding teacher, a gifted stage director
with a particular interest in musical theater, and a highly effective chairperson of
the Department of Theater from 1978 to 1982. Payne's plays for young people,
such as The Strolling Players and his adaptation of Charles Dickens' A Christ-
mas Carol, which have been produced at the University and elsewhere, demon-
strate his skill and talent as a playwright.
It is not insignificant that Payne is a native of Carbondale, in Southern Illinois,
and he returns home for several months each year to write. He is an outstanding
product of SIUC, having earned undergraduate and graduate degrees in the ar-
eas of fine arts and theater. In his letter of nomination, Chair Christian H. Moe of
the SIUC Department of Theater and an SIUC faculty member for 37 years, had
high praise for Payne's accomplishments: "He has earned a sufficient reputation
in his field as an artist, author, and scholar to merit nomination for an honorary
degree in fine arts. He has my unreserved recommendation for this degree".
In recognition of his contributions to the world of theater and of his service to
the region of his youth, Southern Illinois University at Carbondale finds it fitting
and proper to present the honorary degree Doctor of Fine Arts to Darwin Reid
Payne.

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods — the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft tarns
are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no hood is
worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study. Doctor's
caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is worn on
the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and are cus-
tomarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men only.
Southern Illinois University School of Medicine graduates wear gowns of ma-
roon, the color of the university, with black velvet borders and bars, and soft,
eight-point black velvet tarns with green tassels. The lining of the hood is maroon
with a white chevron and the velvet border is green, the color of the discipline of
medicine.

Commencement
August 3, 1996
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of
society. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the
nation.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help
students learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor
activities for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to
help themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and
counseling; learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political,
and volunteer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-
on projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into the Arena either by degree candidates or by
guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal with alcohol or other distract-
ing objects.

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods — the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft tarns
are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no hood is
worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study. Doctor's
caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is worn on
the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and are cus-
tomarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men only.
Southern Illinois University School of Medicine graduates wear gowns of ma-
roon, the color of the university, with black velvet borders and bars, and soft,
eight-point black velvet tarns with green tassels. The lining of the hood is maroon
with a white chevron and the velvet border is green, the color of the discipline of
medicine.

Commencement
May 9 and 10, 1997
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into either the Arena or Shryock Auditorium
either by degree candidates or guests. Security personnel will be on hand to deal
with alcohol or other distracting objects.
Commencement
May 9 and 10, 1997
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of so-
ciety. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the na-
tion.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help stu-
dents learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor activi-
ties for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to help
themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and counseling;
learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political, and volun-
teer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-on
projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.

Distinguished Service Award
Emma K. (Katy) Simonds
Katy Simonds, chairman of the board of E.T. Simonds Construction Company of
Carbondale, has been an enthusiastic and dedicated supporter of our University
for over four decades. A member of the SIU Foundation board of directors, she
serves on the Foundation's executive, nominating, and development committees.
She is currently a member of the SIUC College of Business and Administration
External Advisory Committee and a board member of the Friends of WSIU-TV.
Mrs. Simonds' involvement in increasing private support for the University is
extensive. She has been actively involved in the recruitment of new members to
the Chancellor's Council, of which she is a founding member, and her personal fi-
nancial support has earned her membership in the prestigious Delyte W. Morris
Society of the Council. Her spirited involvement in and support for University
activities ranging from the arts to athletics has earned her the respect and admi-
ration of the University community.
Similarly involved in the Carbondale community, Mrs. Simonds is this year's
general chair of the Jackson County United Way Campaign and was co-chair of
the Carbondale Celebration of the Arts Chautauqua event. She has served as
president of the Women's Club of Carbondale, co-chair of the Jackson County
Red Cross, director of the Carbondale Civic Center Authority Board, and chair-
woman of the Artrain Steering Committee. She was a key volunteer in the $1
million Memorial Hospital of Carbondale fund drive.
Among the many organizations in which Katy Simonds has been an active
member are the Carbondale Memorial Hospital Board, special gifts committee of
the Jackson County American Red Cross, Carbondale Clinic Center Authority,
Quality of Life Services, Inc. Advisory Board, Southern Illinois Hospital Services
Board, Southern Illinois Retirement Community Board, and the Carbondale
Presbyterian Retirement Community Board.
In 1987, Katy and Eugene Simonds were named Citizens of the Year by the
Carbondale Chamber of Commerce, and this year, Mrs. Simonds received the
"Woman of the Decade" award at the tenth annual Southern Illinois Women's
Health Conference.
For her outstanding achievements, dedication, and tireless service to the wel-
fare of the University and the greater Carbondale community, Southern Illinois
University at Carbondale finds it fitting and proper to present the Distinguished
Service Award to Katy Simonds.
Distinguished Service Award
Tom Blomquist
Tom Blomquist, a 1972 graduate in Radio-Television, is a very successful writer
and producer in Hollywood. Upon graduation he joined the legendary Hallmark
Hall of Fame television show. Moving to the West Coast, he joined the manage-
ment team of Grant Tinker at Mary Tyler Moore Enterprises before signing a
multi-year contract as a writer for Stephen J. Cannell Productions. He has re-
cently been producing for CBS. He is a very talented, successful and busy Holly-
wood producer. Yet, over the last ten years, he has made significant time avail-
able to this University and to its students and has been the driving force behind
the creation of Hollywood Studies, a very successful internship program in Ra-
dio-Television.
Since 1988, Mr. Blomquist has returned to campus every year to participate in
Radio-Television Week, delivering seminars on Hollywood production, conduct-
ing a writing workshop, and working with students in establishing networks in
Hollywood and within the profession. His production session usually goes on all
day Saturday and always plays to a standing room crowd of students and faculty
from many different campus disciplines.
It was during these sessions that he conceived the idea of a summer internship
in California for students. The program, Hollywood Studies, commenced opera-
tion with 38 students in summer 1995 and continued with 56 students in summer
1996. It is an eight- week, hands-on internship that includes weekly industry sem-
inars. The quality of the internships and the content of the seminars are the key
to the success of this program. Mr. Blomquist has ensured both.
For two years he has dropped almost everything to help get this program up
and running. He used his own industry relationships to line up exceptional in-
ternships with Chicago Hope; Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman; Walker, Texas
Ranger; and numerous others. Mr. Blomquist also designed the weekly seminars
and recruited the speakers. One such contact resulted in excellent media cover-
age for the University: the Los Angeles-based entertainment editor for the
Chicago Tribune visited the program and filed a feature story in September 1996
that stimulated recruitment efforts and enhanced the image of the University in
the Chicagoland area.
Hollywood Studies is but the latest of many enormous contributions Mr.
Blomquist has made to this institution. He has helped chart a meaningful new
course for our students at some considerable expense to himself. On his own, he
has recruited and coordinated the involvement of other California alumni. The
Department of Radio-Television named him Alumnus of the Year for 1994. His
continuing commitment to helping students complete programs is a positive re-
flection on him and a tremendous asset to SIUC students.
For his commitment and service to the University and its students, Southern
Illinois University at Carbondale finds it fitting and proper to present the Dis-
tinguished Service Award to Tom Blomquist.
Honorary Degree
Doctor of Humane Letters
Nobuo Kumakura
Nobuo Kumakura, Mayor of Nakajo Town in Niigata Prefecture, Japan, is a man
of vision whose bold leadership made the SIUC campus in Japan a reality nine
years ago. Mayor Kumakura has worked hard over the past decade establishing a
positive working relationship between his community and Southern Illinois Uni-
versity at Carbondale. The culmination of this effort has been the establishment
of the Southern Illinois University at Carbondale Nakajo campus.
Through his ability to communicate the long-term benefits of U.S. higher edu-
cation to the Nakajo Town and Niigata Prefecture, millions of dollars were in-
vested to build the Japan campus. Classrooms, dormitories, faculty housing, a li-
brary, and the Illinois-Niigata Friendship Hall — with a bookstore, an auditorium,
and a restaurant — were part of the construction project. Each year a grant is
awarded to SIUC to deliver intensive English and core curriculum courses to
Japanese students. The town provides all maintenance and support of the physi-
cal infrastructure. This represents four to five million dollars each year to pro-
vide an American education for Japanese students planning to study in the
United States. Over 600 students have completed programs in Nakajo and trans-
ferred to Carbondale, where 334 have successfully graduated from SIUC. These
students return to Japan to work in large corporations, teach, and serve as prin-
cipals of high schools and presidents of colleges.
Now in the his last term, Mayor Kumakura is working with SIUC to design an
academic program for our tenth year in Nakajo that will meet the challenge of fu-
ture decades. Only six universities remain of the original 32 programs established
in Japan nine years ago. Without question, the mayor's commitment to education
and his leadership abilities will be the key to securing a long-lasting SIUC pro-
gram in Japan.
During negotiations begun recently, he proposed a plan that would incorporate
distance learning programs to reach high school students, preparing them to at-
tend universities, and to assure our Japanese students a smooth transition into
the mainstream of campus life in Carbondale. His ideas are innovative, and defi-
nitely speak to the future needs and expectations of students.
During May 1997, the tenth-year contract will be signed between SIUC and
Nakajo. Because of the importance of this event, Mayor Kumakura will travel to
Carbondale for a formal signing. Mayor Kumakura has worked tirelessly to im-
prove the educational opportunities for his Japanese students in partnership with
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale. This effort has moved SIUC into the
forefront in international education and continues to reflect well upon our pro-
gramming.
In recognition of his contribution to the field of education and of his service to
Japan and the university, Southern Illinois University finds it fitting and proper
to present the honorary degree Doctor of Humane Letters to Nobuo Kumakura.
Honorary DegTee
Doctor of Humane Letters
Philip Pfeffer
Philip Pfeffer, president and chief operating officer of Random House, Inc., (New
York), has demonstrated outstanding achievement in his field and has exempli-
fied continuing commitment to Southern Illinois University at Carbondale . He is
a two-degree graduate of SIUC. In his present assignment, he is the lead of the
world's largest English-language general trade book publishing house. Mr. Pfef-
fer is indeed an outstanding graduate of our University and has been supportive
of the University over the years.
Mr. Pfeffer has expressed his pride in being the type of student SIUC tradi-
tionally has aimed to educate — one who could not afford college. Aware of the
tradition of providing access to education through financial aid, he saw SIUC as
his opportunity to get an education. He received an activity award scholarship,
and that, along with student work jobs delivering the student newspaper and
working in a residence-hall payroll office, supported him while he completed the
B.A. degree in mathematics in 1965 and the M.A. degree in economics in 1966.
Mr. Pfeffer rose to his first corporate presidency at the age of 25. In 1968 he
took a job as an economist with Genesco Inc., of Nashville, Tennessee; two years
later he became president of one of the firm's subsidiaries, Genesco Export Com-
pany. In 1977, he moved on to the family-owned Ingram Book Company of
Nashville, becoming its president and chief executive officer in just one year. Re-
cast as the Ingram Distribution Group, Inc., the company added pre-recorded
videocassette and microcomputer products to its trade-book distribution. Mr.
Pfeffer is credited with turning Ingram into the world's largest distributor of all
three products. In 1981, Pfeffer was named vice president, board member, and
executive committee member of Ingram Industries, the distribution group's par-
ent company. Ingram Industries was ranked by Forbes in 1994 as America's
ninth largest privately held company, with annual revenues of $11 billion. The
firm also has interests in barge transportation, insurance, petroleum equipment
manufacture, and oil field services.
In addition to his success in the corporate world, he has served on boards for
the University's College of Business and Administration, the SIU Foundation,
and the SIU Alumni Association. In 1989 he received the College of Liberal Arts
Outstanding Alumnus Award. His commitment to the University is reflected in
endowments to benefit Morris Library and the College of Liberal Arts which he
and his wife Pamela have established.
In recognition of his contributions and outstanding achievements in his chosen
field of endeavor and for his continuing commitment to the University, Southern
Illinois University at Carbondale finds it fitting and proper to present the hon-
orary degree of Doctor of Humane Letters to Philip M. Pfeffer.
Candidates for Degrees
The following lists contain the names of candidates for degrees, the granting of
which is contingent upon successful completion of all requirements for the de-
gree.
An asterisk (*) to the right of the name indicates membership in the University
Honors program (undergraduate students only).
University Academic Honors listed to the right of the name are as follows for
undergraduate students:
cum laude 3.5-3.74
magna cum laude 3.75-3.89
summa cum laude 3.9-4.0
The averages above apply to all work taken at Southern Illinois University at
Carbondale and in the case of transfer students to the total work as well.

Academic Regalia
The academic regalia, consisting of cap, gown, and hood, originated about the
twelfth century and was worn primarily for warmth. Later, the material of the
gown and lining and shape of the hood represented the economic and social as
well as the academic status of the wearer.
In 1895, a commission of American educators established an inter-collegiate
code for the academic regalia. This code, revised in 1932 and again in 1960, pro-
vides a comprehensive system of academic regalia for American colleges and uni-
versities. While the code specifies black gowns, foreign universities and a grow-
ing number of American universities have gowns of various colors.
There are three types of gowns and hoods — the bachelor's, master's, and doc-
tor's. The bachelor's gown is untrimmed and has a closed front and long pointed
sleeves. Women may wear a white collar with the bachelor's gown when no hood
is worn. The master's gown is untrimmed, may be worn open or closed, and has
extremely long, closed sleeves with an opening at the wrist. The end of the
sleeves are square with an arc extending from the wrist opening to the square
end. The doctor's gown may be worn open or closed and has round, bell-shaped
sleeves. There are wide velvet borders down the front and three velvet bars on
each sleeve; the borders and bars may be black or the color of the discipline of the
degree.
The hood for each degree has a distinctive form. The bachelor's hood is three
feet in length and has a narrow velvet edging with little of the lining exposed.
The master's hood is three and one-half feet in length with wider velvet edging
and more of the lining exposed. The doctor's hood is four feet in length with the
widest velvet edging and full exposure of the lining. Hoods are lined with the
color(s) of the college or university conferring the degree. The color of the velvet
edging identifies the discipline of the degree.
The black mortarboard cap is standard in the United States, although soft tarns
are worn at some universities. Tassels are usually black, except when no hood is
worn, in which case the color of the tassel represents the field of study. Doctor's
caps may have gold tassels. Upon conferral of the degree the tassel is worn on
the left of the cap. Caps are considered part of the academic regalia and are cus-
tomarily removed only during prayer, oath, or pledge, and then by men only.

Commencement
August 2, 1997
The commencement ceremony is an important occasion not only for you but for
other graduates, families, and friends. Although it is a happy time, it should not
be a time of revelry. Your conduct at the ceremony should be dignified. Alcoholic
beverages may not be brought into either the Student Center Ballrooms or
Shryock Auditorium either by degree candidates or guests. Security personnel
will be on hand to deal with alcohol or other distracting objects.
Southern Illinois University at Carbondale
When its doors were first opened in 1874, Southern Illinois University at Car-
bondale was a place where teachers and scholars believed that their graduates
should be prepared to make useful contributions to the health and strength of so-
ciety. This is still our intention. Outstanding departments, dedicated faculty,
thorough and often inspired instruction, and a thoughtful blending of old wisdom
with new knowledge have become the hallmarks of the University.
Because this is true, we can point with pride to our alumni, many of whom are
distinguished scholars, business leaders, artists, and public servants, and many
more of whom are essential to organizations and communities throughout the na-
tion.
Knowing that classroom learning is only one facet of education, we help stu-
dents learn to play through intramural sports, training in crafts, outdoor activi-
ties for individuals and groups, a variety of musical organizations; learn to help
themselves through wellness education, physical fitness training, and counseling;
learn to help others through fraternal, community service, political, and volun-
teer groups; learn to see and know their surroundings through hands-on
projects, field trips, lectures, and excursions of their own.
In encouraging students to explore the avenues and byways of knowledge and
experience, our aim is to expand their view of the world in such a way that, while
they focus on the particulars of their careers, they will be able to see their lives
and their work in the broad context of the communities and the world they will
be inhabiting.
